lessons.question: A workflow dashboard shows only completed cases, and it looks great. What could it be hiding?
options: Nothing, because completed work is all that matters
A second dashboard with the same data
Stuck or failed work that never finished
lessons.explanation: Every input needs a visible outcome. Showing only completions hides the cases that are waiting, stuck or failed, which are exactly the ones needing attention.

lessons.after: Use explicit states such as received,
lessons.prompt: Put these states in order for a case that goes smoothly through review.
lessons.explanation: Naming each state makes it obvious where a case is waiting. Persisting the state before acknowledging the work means nothing is lost if the process stops.

lessons.question: A reviewer approves a draft reply. Someone then edits a sentence in it. What happens to the approval?
options: The edited version needs a new decision
The approval still stands for the new text
Only the edit needs to be logged
lessons.explanation: Approval applies to an exact versioned payload. Any later change means the reviewer has not seen what will actually be sent.

lessons.prompt: Which statements describe the course simulator, and which go beyond what it claims?

items.text: It uses separate workflow and provider databases
It crashes on purpose after the provider's effect
A retry reuses the same action key and payload hash
It guarantees exactly-once delivery to any service
It puts the remote action inside the local transaction

lessons.explanation: The simulator is a controlled demonstration. A local transaction covers only the local database, never an action on someone else's system.

lessons.question: A reviewer sees a box that just says 'Continue?' before a tool changes an external system. Is that enough to approve safely?
options: Yes, the reviewer can trust the flow
Yes, as long as it appears quickly
No, they need to see the actual proposed arguments
lessons.explanation: A reviewer can only judge what they can see. Showing the exact tool arguments turns a rubber stamp into a real decision.

lessons.after: In n8n, start with a manual execution
lessons.question: In the lab flow, which n8n node routes review-required items down a separate path?
lessons.explanation: Edit Fields supplies the fictional ticket and its event ID, while the If node branches items that need review away from the normal path.

lessons.after: Build the first flow as intake, validation,
lessons.prompt: Arrange the stages of the first lab flow.
lessons.explanation: Checking input before classifying, and reviewing before recording, keeps bad data and unreviewed drafts out of the record. There is deliberately no customer-send step yet.

lessons.prompt: After the A17 crash, is each retry choice safe or a problem?

items.text: Retry with a brand-new action ID
Retry A17 with the identical payload to an idempotent provider
Silently accept a retry of A17 with changed content
Reject a retry of A17 whose content has changed

lessons.explanation: Reusing the same key and payload lets the provider return the existing effect. A new ID creates a duplicate, and changed content was never approved.

lessons.prompt: Your flow fails halfway through a busy Monday. What would you want staff to be able to see?
lessons.answer: Which items are waiting or failed, why, who owns each one, and how old the oldest unresolved item is. A failed item should stay visible with a reason, not vanish into an empty success response.

lessons.after: Use the review prototype to practise approve,
lessons.prompt: Predict each test result: should the simulated provider end up with one effect or none?

items.text: Approved action that runs without any crash
Payload edited after approval and not re-approved
The same approved event is delivered twice

lessons.explanation: Only an approved, unchanged, unexpired payload should take effect, and a repeated delivery of the same event must not add a second effect.

lessons.question: A real recipient has no idempotency support. What should your runbook avoid promising?
options: That uncertain outcomes are checked by a person
Automatic recovery the integration cannot actually provide
That failed items stay visible with an owner
lessons.explanation: A runbook should describe limits as well as successes. Promising recovery the integration cannot deliver sets staff up to create duplicates.
